messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan, a 29-year-old European American man who worked in sales, had been camping alone in a wooded area near a lake when the storm hit. He had gone there for a weekend to clear his head after a difficult stretch at work, choosing the site because it felt quiet and open, away from phones and obligations. Late that evening the weather turned with little warning. He remembered the sky shifting dark, the wind picking up through the trees, and then the frightening rush of realizing how quickly the water around him was rising. In the aftermath, when he tried to explain what had happened, there were parts he simply could not account for no matter how many times he went over the sequence in his mind. What he could remember returned with the same terror he had felt in the moment: the panic, the helplessness, the sense that he was exposed in a place that had seemed peaceful only hours earlier. Even months later, he would sometimes be overtaken by the full force of that dread without seeing a clear picture in his mind, as if the fear itself came first and the memory followed behind.

At first Ethan tried to treat the experience as something he should be able to put behind him, but the days after the storm brought a lasting sense that he no longer knew himself in the same way. He had once seen himself as self-sufficient and steady, yet now he felt unsettled by his own reactions and embarrassed by how easily he startled or checked his surroundings. He came to believe he could not rely on other people in the way he once had, and that belief grew sharper whenever he thought about how alone he had been when the weather changed. Friends offered reassurance, but he found himself keeping them at a distance, not because he wanted to be difficult, but because trusting anyone else to notice danger in time felt naïve to him. Over the months, he also found that nothing in his life felt especially meaningful anymore. He continued to go through the motions of work and errands, but the sense of purpose he had once attached to his plans had thinned, leaving him feeling as though he was moving through days that no longer quite belonged to him.

Certain situations brought the experience rushing back in immediate, bodily ways. Being in natural environments similar to the place where it happened was especially hard, and he began to avoid the lakefront and wooded trails he had once liked. Even driving past physical locations that resembled the campsite could make his body tense before he had fully registered why. At work, as a salesperson, he spent much of his day moving between offices, storefronts, and parking lots, and he noticed that any unfamiliar open space could leave him on edge, scanning exits and weather conditions with a vigilance that exhausted him. He became especially unsettled when he felt emotionally vulnerable, because that state seemed to strip away whatever control he could muster. In those moments he was more likely to feel as if the danger were close again, and his mind could slip into brief flashback-like states in which he suddenly acted as though the storm were returning, looking around sharply or freezing in place before he could fully orient himself.

At night, Ethan rarely slept without disruption. He would wake during the night to check whether he was safe, sometimes sitting upright and listening for sounds that would tell him he was in danger. He kept a charged phone nearby, checked weather alerts more often than he wanted to admit, and would get up to look out the window if the wind changed. During the day he remained superalert, watching the sky, the trees, and the people around him in a way that made it difficult to settle into ordinary routines. The pattern had begun to affect his work as a salesperson in quieter but unmistakable ways: he arrived tired, found it harder to concentrate during client meetings, and sometimes shortened conversations so he could get back to the familiar security of indoor spaces. What finally brought him to seek help was the accumulation of these nights and days, and the growing fear that he was becoming someone entirely unfamiliar to himself. He said he wanted to sleep without waking in a panic, to walk outside without feeling as if the air itself might turn against him, and to find some way to live that did not feel stripped of meaning.
